claim: rfng expression marks hindbrain boundary cells.
source: We found that rfng expression which marks hindbrain boundary cells occurs in epha4-expressing cells at the borders of r3 and r5 (Figure 1A,B,C–C'').
evidence: Supported by in situ HCR analysis showing rfng expression pattern at boundaries (Figure 1A,B,C-C'') and previous literature citation (Cheng et al., 2004).

claim: rfng expression occurs in epha4-expressing cells at the borders of r3 and r5.
source: We found that rfng expression which marks hindbrain boundary cells occurs in epha4-expressing cells at the borders of r3 and r5 (Figure 1A,B,C–C'').
evidence: Demonstrated by HCR co-staining showing rfng and epha4 expression overlap at r3 and r5 borders in Figure 1A,B,C-C''.

claim: rfng expression is detected in a few cells that are not expressing epha4, most consistently found at the lateral edge of the r5/r6 border.
source: rfng expression is also detected in a few cells that are not expressing epha4, which are most consistently found at the lateral edge of the r5/r6 border (arrow in Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Observed in HCR staining data shown in Figure 1A,B with arrow indicating rfng+ epha4- cells.

claim: wnt1 is expressed in the roof plate and in the dorsal part of hindbrain boundaries.
source: We also analysed expression of wnt1, which is expressed in the roof plate and in the dorsal part of hindbrain boundaries (Figure 1D).
evidence: Shown by in situ analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: wnt1 expression in boundaries occurs predominantly in epha4-expressing cells.
source: We found that wnt1 expression in boundaries also occurs predominantly in epha4-expressing cells (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-expression analysis in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Boundary cell formation occurs in cells in which forward signaling is occurring.
source: Boundary cell formation thus occurs in cells in which forward signaling is occurring.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that boundary markers (rfng, wnt1) are expressed in epha4-expressing cells where forward signaling occurs.

claim: Forward signaling of EphA4 is required for border sharpening in the zebrafish hindbrain.
source: We show that forward signaling of EphA4 is required for border sharpening and induction of boundary cells in the zebrafish hindbrain, which we find both require kinase-dependent signaling, with a lesser input of PDZ domain-dependent signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated through analysis of multiple epha4 mutants (null, Δ651, KD, ΔPDZBD) showing border sharpening defects.

claim: Forward signaling of EphA4 is required for induction of boundary cells in the zebrafish hindbrain.
source: We show that forward signaling of EphA4 is required for border sharpening and induction of boundary cells in the zebrafish hindbrain, which we find both require kinase-dependent signaling, with a lesser input of PDZ domain-dependent signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated through analysis of epha4 mutants showing loss or reduction of boundary marker expression (rfng, wnt1, sema3gb).

claim: Border sharpening and boundary cell induction both require kinase-dependent signaling.
source: We show that forward signaling of EphA4 is required for border sharpening and induction of boundary cells in the zebrafish hindbrain, which we find both require kinase-dependent signaling, with a lesser input of PDZ domain-dependent signaling.
evidence: Shown by analysis of epha4KD mutant which has major decrease in boundary marker expression and border sharpness.

claim: Border sharpening and boundary cell induction have a lesser input of PDZ domain-dependent signaling.
source: We show that forward signaling of EphA4 is required for border sharpening and induction of boundary cells in the zebrafish hindbrain, which we find both require kinase-dependent signaling, with a lesser input of PDZ domain-dependent signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of epha4ΔPDZBD mutant showing mild decrease in rfng expression and border sharpness.

claim: Boundary-specific gene expression is regulated by myosin II phosphorylation.
source: We find that boundary-specific gene expression is regulated by myosin II phosphorylation, which increases actomyosin contraction downstream of EphA4 signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by mypt1 knockdown increasing boundary marker expression and blebbistatin treatment decreasing it.

claim: Myosin II phosphorylation increases actomyosin contraction downstream of EphA4 signaling.
source: We find that boundary-specific gene expression is regulated by myosin II phosphorylation, which increases actomyosin contraction downstream of EphA4 signaling.
evidence: Supported by detection of pMLC at boundaries, loss of pMLC in epha4 mutants, and known role of pMLC in actomyosin contraction.

claim: Myosin phosphorylation leads to nuclear translocation of Taz.
source: Myosin phosphorylation leads to nuclear translocation of Taz, which together with Tead1a is required for boundary marker expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased nuclear Taz at boundaries, loss of nuclear Taz in epha4 mutants, and increased nuclear Taz after mypt1 knockdown.

claim: Taz together with Tead1a is required for boundary marker expression.
source: Myosin phosphorylation leads to nuclear translocation of Taz, which together with Tead1a is required for boundary marker expression.
evidence: Shown by loss of boundary marker expression after taz and tead1a knockout.

claim: Actomyosin contraction maintains sharp borders.
source: Since actomyosin contraction maintains sharp borders, there is direct coupling of border sharpness to boundary cell induction that ensures correct organisation of signaling centres.
evidence: Supported by previous work (Calzolari et al., 2014) showing actomyosin cable maintains straight borders.

claim: There is direct coupling of border sharpness to boundary cell induction that ensures correct organisation of signaling centres.
source: Since actomyosin contraction maintains sharp borders, there is direct coupling of border sharpness to boundary cell induction that ensures correct organisation of signaling centres.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that the same pathway (EphA4 → pMLC → actomyosin contraction) regulates both border sharpness and boundary cell formation.

claim: Knockdown of epha4 or ephrinb3 leads to loss or decrease in expression of boundary cell markers at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders.
source: Knockdown of epha4 or ephrinb3 leads to loss or decrease in expression of boundary cell markers at three borders where they interact (Figure 2A): r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 (Terriente et al., 2012); there is potential functional redundancy with ephb4 and ephrinb2 at the r4/r5 border (Chan et al., 2001; Cooke et al., 2001; Cooke et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Terriente et al., 2012) and current data in Figure 2.

claim: The null mutant of epha4 has loss of rfng expression at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders.
source: We found that the null mutant of epha4 has the same phenotype described previously for epha4 knockdown, with loss of rfng expression at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders (Figure 2E; compare with wild type, Figure 2C).
evidence: Shown by in situ hybridization in Figure 2E compared to control in Figure 2C.

claim: Expression of wnt1 and sema3gb was disrupted at r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders in epha4 null mutants.
source: Furthermore, expression of other boundary markers, including wnt1 and sema3gb, was disrupted at these borders (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: A milder disruption of rfng expression at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders is found in ephrinB3 null mutant embryos.
source: A milder disruption of rfng expression at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders is found in ephrinB3 null mutant embryos (Figure 2D), likely reflecting some functional overlap with ephrinB2 which is also a ligand for EphA4 (Cooke et al., 2005).
evidence: Shown by in situ data in Figure 2D and supported by previous work (Cooke et al., 2005) on ephrinB2 as EphA4 ligand.

claim: The epha4Δ651 truncation mutant has the same loss of rfng expression as epha4 null mutants.
source: The epha4Δ651 truncation mutant was found to have the same loss of rfng expression as epha4 null mutants (Figure 2F), supporting the idea that boundary cell formation is dependent upon EphA4 forward signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ analysis in Figure 2F showing loss of rfng at specific boundaries.

claim: The epha4KD mutant has a major decrease, but not complete loss of rfng expression at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders.
source: To address whether kinase-dependent forward signaling is required, we analysed the epha4KD mutant and found a major decrease, but not complete loss of rfng expression at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders (Figure 2G).
evidence: Shown by in situ analysis in Figure 2G.

claim: The residual rfng expression at the r5/r6 border in epha4KD mutants occurs in epha4-expressing cells.
source: The residual rfng expression at the r5/r6 border occurs in epha4-expressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G,G'), arguing against the possibility that it is due to reverse signaling activated by epha4KD.
evidence: Demonstrated by HCR co-staining in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G,G'.

claim: The epha4ΔPDZBD mutant has a mild decrease in rfng expression at the r2/r3 and r5/r6 borders, though not at the r3/r4 border.
source: We found that there is a mild decrease in rfng expression at the r2/r3 and r5/r6 borders, though not at the r3/r4 border (Figure 2H).
evidence: Shown by in situ analysis in Figure 2H with quantitation provided in figure legend.

claim: The epha4 null mutant has a decrease in sharpness of the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders.
source: Analysis of egr2 expression in the epha4 null mutant revealed a decrease in sharpness of the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders, with some egr2-expressing cells in the adjacent segments (Figure 2K; compare with control, Figure 2I).
evidence: Demonstrated by egr2 in situ analysis in Figure 2K showing ectopic cells compared to control in Figure 2I.

claim: The sharpness of the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders was disrupted in the ephrinb3, epha4Δ651 and epha4KD mutants.
source: The sharpness of the same borders was disrupted in the ephrinb3, epha4Δ651 and epha4KD mutants, though with fewer ectopic egr2-expressing cells compared with the null mutant (Figure 2J,L,M).
evidence: Shown by egr2 in situ analysis in Figure 2J,L,M.

claim: In the epha4ΔPDZBD mutant there was a decrease in sharpness at the r5/r6 border but only in 30% of the embryos at r2/r3.
source: In the epha4ΔPDZBD mutant there was a decrease in sharpness at the r5/r6 border but only in 30% of the embryos at r2/r3 (Figure 2N).
evidence: Demonstrated by egr2 analysis in Figure 2N with quantitation in legend.

claim: There is a correlation between decreased border sharpness and decreased boundary marker expression.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that both kinase-dependent and PDZ domain-dependent pathways contribute to upregulation of boundary marker expression, with a stronger input of kinase signaling. There is a correlation between decreased border sharpness and decreased boundary marker expression, suggestive of a mechanistic link.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mutants with decreased border sharpness also have decreased boundary marker expression.

claim: EphA4 signaling regulates formation of an actin cable at boundaries, which is first detected at 15 hpf.
source: EphA4 signaling regulates formation of an actin cable at boundaries, which is first detected at 15 hpf and has been implicated in maintenance of a straight border through actomyosin-dependent generation of cortical tension (Calzolari et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Calzolari et al., 2014) on actin cable formation and function.

claim: The actin cable at boundaries has been implicated in maintenance of a straight border through actomyosin-dependent generation of cortical tension.
source: EphA4 signaling regulates formation of an actin cable at boundaries, which is first detected at 15 hpf and has been implicated in maintenance of a straight border through actomyosin-dependent generation of cortical tension (Calzolari et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Calzolari et al., 2014).

claim: Hindbrain boundary cells have a distinct shape from non-boundary cells.
source: Hindbrain boundary cells have a distinct shape from non-boundary cells, which is altered by knockdown of the myosin phosphatase regulator, mypt1, that leads to increased phosphorylation of myosin light chain (pMLC) and actomyosin contraction (Figure 3H) (Gutzman and Sive, 2010).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Gutzman and Sive, 2010) and schematic in Figure 3H.

claim: Knockdown of mypt1 leads to increased phosphorylation of myosin light chain (pMLC) and actomyosin contraction.
source: Hindbrain boundary cells have a distinct shape from non-boundary cells, which is altered by knockdown of the myosin phosphatase regulator, mypt1, that leads to increased phosphorylation of myosin light chain (pMLC) and actomyosin contraction (Figure 3H) (Gutzman and Sive, 2010).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Gutzman and Sive, 2010) and known function of Mypt1 as phosphatase regulator.

claim: There is a higher level of pMLC co-localising with the actin cable at hindbrain borders.
source: Consistent with these findings, we found a higher level of pMLC co-localising with the actin cable at hindbrain borders (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining for actin and pMLC in Figure 3A,B.

claim: pMLC was no longer detected at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders in epha4 null mutants.
source: Furthermore, pMLC was no longer detected at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders in epha4 null mutants (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Shown by pMLC immunostaining in epha4 null mutants in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Knockdown or transient CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of mypt1 leads to an increase in the level and width of rfng expression at hindbrain boundaries.
source: Surprisingly, we found that knockdown or transient CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of mypt1 leads to an increase in the level and width of rfng expression at hindbrain boundaries (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ analysis in Figure 3E–G showing increased rfng after mypt1 knockdown/knockout.

claim: mypt1 knockdown leads to increased expression of wnt1 and sema3gb at boundaries.
source: Likewise, mypt1 knockdown leads to increased expression of wnt1 and sema3gb at boundaries (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Shown by in situ analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: rfng expression after mypt1 knockdown spreads only into the epha4-expressing domain where forward signaling is occurring.
source: By carrying out in situ HCR we found that rfng expression spreads only into the epha4-expressing domain where forward signaling is occurring (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: Demonstrated by HCR co-staining for rfng and epha4 in mypt1 knockdown embryos in Figure 3I–L.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment from 15 hpf onwards strongly disrupts the upregulation of rfng expression at boundaries.
source: We found that blebbistatin treatment from 15 hpf onwards strongly disrupts the upregulation of rfng expression at boundaries, with a progressively milder effect on the expression when the treatment is started at later times, and no change detected when treated from 18 hpf (Figure 3M–P).
evidence: Demonstrated by blebbistatin treatment experiments shown in Figure 3M–P.

claim: Disruption of actin polymerisation by treating embryos with latrunculinB leads to loss of rfng expression at boundaries.
source: Furthermore, disruption of actin polymerisation by treating embryos with latrunculinB leads to loss of rfng expression at boundaries (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Shown by HCR staining after latrunculinB treatment in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: mypt1 knockdown in epha4 null mutants rescues rfng expression at the r2/r3 and r3/4 borders, but not at the r5/r6 border.
source: We found that mypt1 knockdown in epha4 null mutants rescues rfng expression at the r2/r3 and r3/4 borders, but not at the r5/r6 border (Figure 4C,H; wild type embryos in Figure 4A,F; quantitated in Figure 4K).
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ analysis in Figure 4C,H with quantitation in Figure 4K.

claim: mypt1 knockdown rescues rfng expression at the r5/r6 border as well as the r2/r3 and r3/r4 borders in the epha4Δ651 and epha4KD mutants.
source: Intriguingly, mypt1 knockdown rescues rfng expression at the r5/r6 border as well as the r2/r3 and r3/r4 borders in the epha4Δ651 and epha4KD mutants (Figure 4D,E,I–K).
evidence: Shown by in situ analysis in Figure 4D,E,I–K.

claim: mypt1 knockdown rescues rfng expression at all hindbrain boundaries in ephrinB3 null mutants.
source: mypt1 knockdown rescues rfng expression at all hindbrain boundaries in ephrinB3 null mutants (Figure 4B,G), consistent with residual EphA4 activation by other ephrins.
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ analysis in Figure 4B,G.

claim: Knockdown of the taz gene disrupts boundary marker expression, including rfng, wnt1 and sema3gb.
source: This screen revealed that knockdown of the taz gene disrupts boundary marker expression, including rfng, wnt1 and sema3gb (Figure 5A,B,H; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Shown by morpholino knockdown experiments in Figure 5A,B,H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: Transient CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletions of taz lead to decreased rfng expression at boundaries.
source: To test the specificity of the gene knockdown, we carried out transient CRISPR/Cas9-mediated deletions of taz and found that this also leads to decreased rfng expression at boundaries (Figure 5C,H).
evidence: Demonstrated by CRISPR knockout experiments in Figure 5C,H.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of the yap1 gene has little effect on boundary marker expression.
source: In contrast, knockdown or knockout of the related yap1 gene has little effect on boundary marker expression (Figure 5D,E,H), albeit this could reflect that loss of function is not complete.
evidence: Shown by morpholino and CRISPR experiments in Figure 5D,E,H.

claim: taz has a non-redundant role in upregulation of boundary marker expression.
source: The strong effect of taz loss of function suggests that it has a non-redundant role in upregulation of boundary marker expression.
evidence: Inferred from the strong phenotype of taz knockdown/knockout compared to yap1.

claim: Knockout of tead1a leads to a decrease in rfng expression.
source: We found that knockout of tead1a, but not of tead3, leads to a decrease in rfng expression (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by transient CRISPR knockout in Figure 5F–H.

claim: Knockout of tead3 does not lead to a decrease in rfng expression.
source: We found that knockout of tead1a, but not of tead3, leads to a decrease in rfng expression (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: Shown by transient CRISPR knockout in Figure 5F–H.

claim: There is an increased level of Taz, accompanied by nuclear localisation in some cells, at hindbrain boundaries, starting at 14 hpf and becoming more prominent at 18 hpf.
source: We found an increased level of Taz, accompanied by nuclear localisation in some cells, at hindbrain boundaries, starting at 14 hpf and becoming more prominent at 18 hpf (Figure 6A–C,J; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Taz immunostaining time course in Figure 6A–C,J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no longer nuclear Taz staining at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders in epha4 null mutants.
source: We found that there is no longer nuclear Taz staining at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders, whereas the increased level of Taz and nuclear localisation remains at the r1/r2, r4/5 and r6/r7 borders, where boundary marker expression occurs in epha4 mutants (Figure 6D,K; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown by Taz immunostaining in epha4 null mutants in Figure 6D,K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nuclear Taz was no longer detected at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders in epha4Δ651 and epha4KD mutants.
source: To determine whether Taz localisation is regulated by forward signaling, we analysed epha4Δ651 and epha4KD mutants and found that nuclear Taz was no longer detected at the r2/r3, r3/r4 and r5/r6 borders (Figure 6E,F; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by Taz immunostaining in epha4Δ651 and epha4KD mutants in Figure 6E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Forward but not reverse signaling leads to nuclear translocation of Taz.
source: These findings suggest that forward but not reverse signaling leads to nuclear translocation of Taz.
evidence: Inferred from loss of nuclear Taz in epha4Δ651 mutant which lacks forward signaling but retains reverse signaling.

claim: mypt1 knockdown leads to an increase in the number of cells with nuclear Taz at segment borders.
source: To test whether Taz localisation is influenced by myosin phosphorylation, we carried out mypt1 knockdown and found that this leads to an increase in the number of cells with nuclear Taz at segment borders (Figure 6G,I,L).
evidence: Demonstrated by Taz immunostaining after mypt1 knockdown in Figure 6G,I,L with quantitation.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment leads to a decrease in nuclear localisation of Taz.
source: Finally, we analysed the effect of decreasing myosin II function by treating embryos with blebbistatin and found a decrease in nuclear localisation of Taz (Figure 6H).
evidence: Shown by Taz immunostaining after blebbistatin treatment in Figure 6H.

claim: pMLC is still elevated at hindbrain boundaries following knockout of Taz.
source: To address this question, we analysed MLC phosphorylation following knockout of Taz, and found that pMLC is still elevated at hindbrain boundaries (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by pMLC immunostaining in taz knockdown embryos in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myosin phosphorylation does not require Taz function.
source: To address this question, we analysed MLC phosphorylation following knockout of Taz, and found that pMLC is still elevated at hindbrain boundaries (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that pMLC is still present at boundaries in taz knockdown embryos.

claim: EphA4 activation leads to actomyosin phosphorylation and contraction at segment borders, which in turn increases nuclear localisation of Taz and boundary marker expression.
source: Taken together, these findings support a model in which EphA4 activation leads to actomyosin phosphorylation and contraction at segment borders, which in turn increases nuclear localisation of Taz and boundary marker expression.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings showing EphA4 → pMLC → nuclear Taz → boundary marker expression pathway.

claim: Sharp borders enable the correct organisation of signaling centres.
source: A key concept that came from early studies of compartment boundaries is that sharp borders enable the correct organisation of signaling centres (Dahmann and Basler, 1999).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Dahmann and Basler, 1999).

claim: Forward signaling of EphA4 regulates myosin light chain phosphorylation that increases cortical tension.
source: We show that forward signaling of EphA4, which regulates myosin light chain phosphorylation that increases cortical tension, is required both for border sharpening and for hindbrain boundary cell formation.
evidence: Demonstrated by loss of pMLC in epha4 mutants and known role of pMLC in cortical tension.

claim: Increasing myosin II phosphorylation by knockdown of mypt1 increases boundary marker expression.
source: Furthermore, increasing myosin II phosphorylation by knockdown of mypt1 increases boundary marker expression, whereas inhibition of myosin II function or actin polymerization blocks boundary marker expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by increased rfng, wnt1, and sema3gb expression after mypt1 knockdown.

claim: Inhibition of myosin II function or actin polymerization blocks boundary marker expression.
source: Furthermore, increasing myosin II phosphorylation by knockdown of mypt1 increases boundary marker expression, whereas inhibition of myosin II function or actin polymerization blocks boundary marker expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by loss of rfng after blebbistatin or latrunculinB treatment.

claim: EphA4 forward signaling and myosin phosphorylation induce nuclear translocation of Taz, which together with Tead1a regulates boundary marker expression.
source: We show that EphA4 forward signaling and myosin phosphorylation induce nuclear translocation of Taz, which together with Tead1a regulates boundary marker expression (Figure 7).
evidence: Demonstrated by loss of nuclear Taz in epha4 mutants, increased nuclear Taz after mypt1 knockdown, and loss of boundary markers after taz/tead1a knockout.

claim: Increased tension underlies the maintenance of a straight border.
source: Since increased tension underlies the maintenance of a straight border (Calzolari et al., 2014), cell segregation and boundary cell formation are coupled, thus ensuring that boundary cells are organised at a sharp border (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Calzolari et al., 2014).

claim: Cell segregation and boundary cell formation are coupled, thus ensuring that boundary cells are organised at a sharp border.
source: Since increased tension underlies the maintenance of a straight border (Calzolari et al., 2014), cell segregation and boundary cell formation are coupled, thus ensuring that boundary cells are organised at a sharp border (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from the finding that the same pathway (actomyosin contraction) regulates both border sharpness and boundary cell formation.

claim: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling has major role in cell segregation and border sharpening in many tissues in vertebrates.
source: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling has major role in cell segregation and border sharpening in many tissues in vertebrates (Batlle and Wilkinson, 2012; Cayuso et al., 2015; Fagotto et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: Eph receptors comprise a large family of receptor tyrosine kinases that are activated upon binding to their membrane-bound ephrin ligands.
source: Eph receptors comprise a large family of receptor tyrosine kinases that are activated upon binding to their membrane-bound ephrin ligands.
evidence: Established knowledge about Eph receptor family.

claim: Members of the EphA subclass bind to the GPI-anchored ephrinA ligands, whereas EphB receptors bind to transmembrane ephrinB ligands.
source: Members of the EphA subclass bind to the GPI-anchored ephrinA ligands, whereas EphB receptors bind to transmembrane ephrinB ligands; an exception is EphA4 which binds to ephrinA and specific ephrinB family members (Gale et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Gale et al., 1996) and established knowledge.

claim: EphA4 binds to ephrinA and specific ephrinB family members.
source: Members of the EphA subclass bind to the GPI-anchored ephrinA ligands, whereas EphB receptors bind to transmembrane ephrinB ligands; an exception is EphA4 which binds to ephrinA and specific ephrinB family members (Gale et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Gale et al., 1996).

claim: Upon interacting through cell-cell contact, Eph receptor and ephrin proteins are clustered and this activates signal transduction through both components, termed forward and reverse signaling, respectively.
source: Upon interacting through cell-cell contact, Eph receptor and ephrin proteins are clustered and this activates signal transduction through both components, termed forward and reverse signaling, respectively (Klein, 2012; Pasquale, 2008).
evidence: Supported by previous studies (Klein, 2012; Pasquale, 2008) and established knowledge.

claim: Eph receptor forward signaling involves kinase-dependent signaling that activates multiple intracellular pathways.
source: For Eph receptors, this involves kinase-dependent signaling that activates multiple intracellular pathways.
evidence: Established knowledge about Eph receptor signaling mechanisms.

claim: Eph receptor signaling is mediated by a motif at the C-terminus that binds to PDZ domain proteins.
source: In addition, signaling is mediated by a motif at the C-terminus of Eph receptors that binds to PDZ domain proteins.
evidence: Established knowledge about Eph receptor signaling mechanisms.

claim: ephrinB signaling occurs through phosphorylation of conserved tyrosine residues by cytoplasmic kinases, and also through interaction of PDZ domain proteins.
source: In the case of ephrinB proteins, signaling occurs through phosphorylation of conserved tyrosine residues by cytoplasmic kinases, and also through interaction of PDZ domain proteins.
evidence: Established knowledge about ephrinB signaling mechanisms.

claim: Eph receptors and ephrins that have a high affinity for each other are expressed in complementary domains in many tissues.
source: Eph receptors and ephrins that have a high affinity for each other are expressed in complementary domains in many tissues (Cayuso et al., 2015; Gale et al., 1996; Rohani et al., 2014), such that activation of forward and reverse signaling occurs at the interface.
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: Activation of forward and reverse signaling occurs at the interface of complementary Eph/ephrin expression domains.
source: Eph receptors and ephrins that have a high affinity for each other are expressed in complementary domains in many tissues (Cayuso et al., 2015; Gale et al., 1996; Rohani et al., 2014), such that activation of forward and reverse signaling occurs at the interface.
evidence: Inferred from complementary expression patterns and contact-dependent activation.

claim: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling can drive cell segregation and border sharpening by decreasing cell-cell adhesion.
source: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling can drive cell segregation and border sharpening through multiple mechanisms that likely depend upon whether the tissue is epithelial or mesenchymal: by decreasing cell-cell adhesion (Fagotto et al., 2013; Solanas et al., 2011), by increasing cortical tension (Calzolari et al., 2014; Canty et al., 2017), or by triggering cell repulsion (Poliakov et al., 2008; Rohani et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Fagotto et al., 2013; Solanas et al., 2011).

claim: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling can drive cell segregation and border sharpening by increasing cortical tension.
source: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling can drive cell segregation and border sharpening through multiple mechanisms that likely depend upon whether the tissue is epithelial or mesenchymal: by decreasing cell-cell adhesion (Fagotto et al., 2013; Solanas et al., 2011), by increasing cortical tension (Calzolari et al., 2014; Canty et al., 2017), or by triggering cell repulsion (Poliakov et al., 2008; Rohani et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Calzolari et al., 2014; Canty et al., 2017).

claim: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling can drive cell segregation and border sharpening by triggering cell repulsion.
source: Eph receptor and ephrin signaling can drive cell segregation and border sharpening through multiple mechanisms that likely depend upon whether the tissue is epithelial or mesenchymal: by decreasing cell-cell adhesion (Fagotto et al., 2013; Solanas et al., 2011), by increasing cortical tension (Calzolari et al., 2014; Canty et al., 2017), or by triggering cell repulsion (Poliakov et al., 2008; Rohani et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Poliakov et al., 2008; Rohani et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).

claim: Eph-ephrin signaling has been found to regulate cell differentiation in a number of tissues.
source: In addition, Eph-ephrin signaling has been found to regulate cell differentiation in a number of tissues (reviewed by Laussu et al., 2014; Wilkinson, 2014).
evidence: Supported by review articles cited (Laussu et al., 2014; Wilkinson, 2014).

claim: The hindbrain is subdivided into segments, termed rhombomeres (r1-r7), each with a distinct anteroposterior identity and demarcated by borders across which cell intermingling is restricted.
source: The hindbrain is subdivided into segments, termed rhombomeres (r1-r7), each with a distinct anteroposterior identity and demarcated by borders across which cell intermingling is restricted (Fraser et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Fraser et al., 1990) and established knowledge.

claim: Hindbrain borders are initially fuzzy and then sharpened through the regulation of cell identity in combination with cell segregation driven by Eph-ephrin signaling.
source: These borders are initially fuzzy and then sharpened through the regulation of cell identity (Addison et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2017) in combination with cell segregation driven by Eph-ephrin signaling (Cooke et al., 2005; Irving et al., 1996; Kemp et al., 2009; Nieto et al., 1992; Xu et al., 1995; Xu et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: Boundary cells are induced to form at segment borders.
source: Boundary cells are induced to form at segment borders (Guthrie and Lumsden, 1991) and express specific molecular markers that distinguish them from non-boundary cells (Cheng et al., 2004; Cooke et al., 2005; Heyman et al., 1995; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: Boundary cells express specific molecular markers that distinguish them from non-boundary cells.
source: Boundary cells are induced to form at segment borders (Guthrie and Lumsden, 1991) and express specific molecular markers that distinguish them from non-boundary cells (Cheng et al., 2004; Cooke et al., 2005; Heyman et al., 1995; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: In zebrafish, boundary cell markers include the Notch modulator, rfng, which by inhibiting neurogenesis promotes the maintenance of boundary cells.
source: In zebrafish, these include the Notch modulator, rfng, which by inhibiting neurogenesis promotes the maintenance of boundary cells (Cheng et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Cheng et al., 2004).

claim: Boundary cells are a source of neuronal progenitor cells in chick.
source: Boundary cells are a source of neuronal progenitor cells in chick (Peretz et al., 2016), and express a number of signaling molecules that may regulate local patterning (Amoyel et al., 2005; Gerety and Wilkinson, 2011; Riley et al., 2004; Sela-Donenfeld et al., 2009; Weisinger et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Peretz et al., 2016).

claim: Boundary cells express a number of signaling molecules that may regulate local patterning.
source: Boundary cells are a source of neuronal progenitor cells in chick (Peretz et al., 2016), and express a number of signaling molecules that may regulate local patterning (Amoyel et al., 2005; Gerety and Wilkinson, 2011; Riley et al., 2004; Sela-Donenfeld et al., 2009; Weisinger et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: In the zebrafish hindbrain, boundary cells organise spatially-restricted neurogenesis within segments by expressing Semaphorin chemorepellants that position fgf20-expressing neurons in each segment centre.
source: In the zebrafish hindbrain, boundary cells organise spatially-restricted neurogenesis within segments by expressing Semaphorin chemorepellants that position fgf20-expressing neurons in each segment centre (Gonzalez-Quevedo et al., 2010; Terriente et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Gonzalez-Quevedo et al., 2010; Terriente et al., 2012).

claim: ephA4 is expressed in r3 and r5.
source: Since epha4 (epha4a) is expressed in r3 and r5 (Xu et al., 1995), and ephrinb3 (efnb3b) in r2, r4 and r6 (Chan et al., 2001), this Eph-ephrin pair interacts at all borders of r3 and r5.
evidence: Supported by previous study (Xu et al., 1995).

claim: ephrinb3 is expressed in r2, r4 and r6.
source: Since epha4 (epha4a) is expressed in r3 and r5 (Xu et al., 1995), and ephrinb3 (efnb3b) in r2, r4 and r6 (Chan et al., 2001), this Eph-ephrin pair interacts at all borders of r3 and r5.
evidence: Supported by previous study (Chan et al., 2001).

claim: The EphA4-ephrinB3 pair interacts at all borders of r3 and r5.
source: Since epha4 (epha4a) is expressed in r3 and r5 (Xu et al., 1995), and ephrinb3 (efnb3b) in r2, r4 and r6 (Chan et al., 2001), this Eph-ephrin pair interacts at all borders of r3 and r5.
evidence: Inferred from complementary expression patterns of epha4 and ephrinb3.

claim: Disruption of Eph receptor or ephrin function leads to a decrease both in the sharpening of segment borders and in the expression of boundary markers.
source: Disruption of Eph receptor or ephrin function leads to a decrease both in the sharpening of segment borders and in the expression of boundary markers (Cooke et al., 2005; Sela-Donenfeld et al., 2009; Terriente et al., 2012; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: EphA4 and ephrinB3 act as a signaling pair since knockdown of either component disrupts the same segment boundaries.
source: EphA4 and ephrinB3 act as a signaling pair since knockdown of either component disrupts the same segment boundaries (Terriente et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Terriente et al., 2012).

claim: Boundary marker expression is up-regulated by forward signaling.
source: We find that boundary cell markers are expressed in epha4-expressing cells and are up-regulated by forward signaling.
evidence: Demonstrated by expression analysis and mutant studies showing loss of boundary markers in forward signaling mutants.

claim: Kinase-dependent and PDZ domain-dependent signaling both contribute to regulation of border sharpening and boundary-specific gene expression.
source: By creating a series of truncation and point mutants in epha4, we show that kinase-dependent and PDZ domain-dependent signaling both contribute to regulation of border sharpening and boundary-specific gene expression.
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of epha4KD and epha4ΔPDZBD mutants showing partial phenotypes.

claim: Mechanotransduction that induces boundary marker expression is mediated by nuclear translocation of Taz.
source: Mechanotransduction that induces boundary marker expression is mediated by nuclear translocation of Taz.
evidence: Demonstrated by nuclear Taz at boundaries, loss of nuclear Taz in epha4 mutants, and loss of boundary markers after taz knockout.

claim: The regulation of actomysosin contraction by Eph signaling couples the maintenance of sharp borders and induction of a boundary signaling centre.
source: The regulation of actomysosin contraction by Eph signaling thus couples the maintenance of sharp borders and induction of a boundary signaling centre.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that actomyosin contraction regulates both border sharpness and boundary marker expression through the same pathway.

claim: Eph kinase-independent signaling can also lead to cell repulsion and segregation.
source: Eph kinase-independent signaling can also lead to cell repulsion and segregation (Taylor et al., 2017) and can activate Rho, for example through binding of Dishevelled to the PDZ domain binding motif of Eph receptors (Tanaka et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Taylor et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2003).

claim: Kinase-independent signaling leads to a less sustained cell repulsion response than occurs when Eph kinase function is intact.
source: Such kinase-independent signaling leads to a less sustained cell repulsion response than occurs when Eph kinase function is intact (Taylor et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Taylor et al., 2017).

claim: Forward signaling leads to much stronger cell repulsion and actomyosin contraction and thus has a dominant role in cell segregation and border sharpening.
source: This finding is consistent with evidence that although reverse signaling can trigger cell repulsion, forward signaling leads to much stronger cell repulsion and actomyosin contraction and thus has a dominant role in cell segregation and border sharpening (Canty et al., 2017; Fagotto et al., 2013; O'Neill et al., 2016; Rohani et al., 2011; Rohani et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: Yap and Taz have been intensively studied as components of a pathway which links mechanical tension to the regulation of cell proliferation.
source: Taz and Yap have been intensively studied as components of a pathway which links mechanical tension to the regulation of cell proliferation (Elbediwy et al., 2016; Gaspar and Tapon, 2014; Halder et al., 2012; Low et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple review articles cited.

claim: Taz and Yap have been implicated in the maintenance of stem cells or regulation of cell differentiation in specific tissues.
source: In addition, Taz and Yap have been implicated in the maintenance of stem cells or regulation of cell differentiation in specific tissues (Chen et al., 2019; Isomursu et al., 2019; Luxenburg and Zaidel-Bar, 2019; Mo et al., 2014; Panciera et al., 2017; Varelas, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.

claim: Mechanical cues or other inputs lead to the translocation of Yap/Taz protein from cytoplasm to the nucleus, where they can interact with Tead family transcription factors to regulate specific gene expression.
source: Mechanical cues or other inputs lead to the translocation of Yap/Taz protein from cytoplasm to the nucleus, where they can interact with Tead family transcription factors to regulate specific gene expression.
evidence: Established knowledge about Yap/Taz mechanotransduction pathway.

claim: tead1a and tead3 are widely expressed in the nervous system, with segmental regulation of the level of expression.
source: Gene expression studies have found that two tead family members, tead1a and tead3, are widely expressed in the nervous system, with segmental regulation of the level of expression (Thisse et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Thisse et al., 2001).

claim: The actin cytoskeleton can regulate the stability as well as nuclear localisation of Taz.
source: These observations are consistent with evidence that the actin cytoskeleton can regulate the stability as well as nuclear localisation of Taz (Dupont et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Dupont et al., 2011).

claim: The Drosophila homologue of Yap/Taz, Yorkie, can increase myosin activity and tension independently of its function as a transcription co-factor.
source: The Drosophila homologue of Yap/Taz, Yorkie, can increase myosin activity and tension independently of its function as a transcription co-factor (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Xu et al., 2018).

claim: Hindbrain boundaries have a lower proliferation rate than segment centres in chick.
source: Studies in chick argue against this idea as hindbrain boundaries have a lower proliferation rate than segment centres (Guthrie et al., 1991; Peretz et al., 2016), reflecting their role as a pool of neurogenic stem cells.
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Guthrie et al., 1991; Peretz et al., 2016).

claim: Recent work has found two-fold greater proliferation at boundaries than segment centres at late stages in the zebrafish hindbrain (after 26 hpf), which depends upon Yap/Taz and Tead activity.
source: However, recent work has found two-fold greater proliferation at boundaries than segment centres at late stages in the zebrafish hindbrain (after 26 hpf), which depends upon Yap/Taz and Tead activity (Voltes et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by recent study (Voltes et al., 2019).

claim: The Yap/Taz-Tead pathway is activated by actomyosin tension at boundaries and increases cell proliferation downstream of Eph-ephrin signaling.
source: Importantly, this work found that the Yap/Taz-Tead pathway is activated by actomyosin tension at boundaries and therefore increases cell proliferation downstream of Eph-ephrin signaling.
evidence: Supported by recent study (Voltes et al., 2019).

claim: Yap/Taz activation and cell proliferation declines by 40 hpf, concommitant with a switch of boundary cells to neurogenesis.
source: Yap/Taz activation and cell proliferation declines by 40 hpf, concommitant with a switch of boundary cells to neurogenesis (Voltes et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by recent study (Voltes et al., 2019).

claim: The mechanical regulation of gene expression enables an interplay between morphogenesis and cell identity that contributes to tissue patterning.
source: The mechanical regulation of gene expression enables an interplay between morphogenesis and cell identity that contributes to tissue patterning (Chan et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2018; Xia et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited.

claim: epha4 expression is regulated by krox20.
source: In the hindbrain, epha4 expression is regulated by krox20 (Theil et al., 1998), such that cell segregation and border sharpening is coupled to segmental identity (Tumpel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Theil et al., 1998; Tumpel et al., 2009).

claim: Cell segregation and border sharpening is coupled to segmental identity.
source: In the hindbrain, epha4 expression is regulated by krox20 (Theil et al., 1998), such that cell segregation and border sharpening is coupled to segmental identity (Tumpel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by previous study (Tumpel et al., 2009).

claim: Eph activation regulates cell fate choices in Ciona by antagonising Fgf signaling through inhibition of the MAPK pathway.
source: For example, Eph activation regulates cell fate choices in Ciona by antagonising Fgf signaling through inhibition of the MAPK pathway (Picco et al., 2007; Stolfi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by previous studies cited (Picco et al., 2007; Stolfi et al., 2011).

claim: The principal mechanisms that drive border sharpening are contact repulsion and cortical tension that require actomyosin contraction.
source: Since the principal mechanisms that drive border sharpening are contact repulsion and cortical tension that require actomyosin contraction (Canty et al., 2017; Fagotto et al., 2013; O'Neill et al., 2016; Rohani et al., 2011; Rohani et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2017), this raises the question as to whether the pathway uncovered here in the hindbrain is deployed in other tissues to regulate gene expression through Yap/Taz activation.
evidence: Supported by multiple previous studies cited.
